title: I Used the Welding-Booth Timer on the Mentor Who Left My Coupons

parts.text: I stepped into booth four at 1:06 p.m. and mentor Pax was already using my numbered coupons. The board said: SIXTY MINUTES. COUPONS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-five, shop steward, holding a clipboard that listed our booth. Pax shrugged. "Mentors hold the arc." I photographed the board, the booking, and his bead on my coupons. Then I asked for the booth timer. At 1:14 the shop desk pinged why Pax's bead sat on our coupons. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The shop desk can see Pax's bead in booth four during our hour.

social.video_title: He left his bead on my numbered coupons — Part 1/2
social.description: Welding booth, a mentor on my coupons, a sixty-minute clock he posted. I logged the bead. Would you have asked for the booth timer?

parts.text: Pax called it practice beads until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the coupon still. The coupons went back to my numbered bin. Pax ran a slot of their own and told the next mentor atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: MENTORS DO NOT HOLD THE ARC. I keep our hour on a labeled card. Pax brown-bags his beads. The booth finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.
